title: The Zong Case: Slavery, Abolition, and the Zong Massacre: Interdisciplinary Perspectives
description: In 1781, 132 slaves on the British slave ship the Zong were thrown overboard enroute from Africa to Jamaica. "The Zong massacre" and resulting insurance dispute played a key role in 18-19th century abolitionist movements. The case is taken up in writings by Clarkson, Equiano, Cugoano, Hazlitt & in a Turner painting, but it has shaped how we understand conditions for modernity broadly, including notions of personhood. Course examines significance of Zong massacre with interdisciplinary perspectives on space & ecology of slave ships, figures of maroons & slavewomen in literature, metaphors of colonial disease. Readings & visuals: 19th century literature (More, Clarkson, Clarke), contemporary reflections (Dabydeen, DAguair, Rankine, Philips).

title: The Devil in Literature
description: Explores the rich literature around making deals with the devil while focusing on the enduring influence of older literature on modern conceptions of the diabolic.

title: Narrative Studies
description: Study of various narrative forms, e.g., novel, short story, essay, memoir, with a specific focus each quarter. Topics to be addressed may include strategies of narration, the history of particular narrative forms, what is meant by literary style.

title: Autobiographies and Life Stories
description: Considers autobiographies, memoirs, testimonials, life writing, and other works of narrative fiction and nonfiction often written in the first person. Topics include self-portrait, the portrayal of childhood and family, childhood and youth narratives, women's autobiography, first-person accounts of illness and disability in comics, and more. Texts and course foci vary with the instructor.

title: Disability and Culture
description: With a view of integrating disability as a critical category into teaching and research, courses approach physical, sensory, and psychological impairments as well as bodily and mental differences in literary, visual, artistic, and popular forms across classical and modern periods. The main fields of study include world literature, art, film studies, philosophy, linguistics, history, and religious studies in conjunction with adjacent fields that help reconfigure the concept of ability and normalcy. Content will vary according to instructors.

title: Disability and Literature
description: Readings of canonical and non-canonical texts (fiction, memoir, poetry) through a variety of critical approaches, covering a wide range of impairments and the innovations that disability requires in literary and artistic forms. Content will vary according to instructors.

title: Fantasy and the Fantastic
description: Course explores the creation of a space where a fantastic perception of reality developed and thrived, hesitating between the real and the supernatural, in the intermediate space of the unexplained and unexplainable. Works by Balzac, Poe, Stevenson, James, and Borges.

title: VIOLENCE AS DE-COLONIZING CATHARSIS:FROM FRANTZ FANON TO THE TRICONTINENTAL MANIFESTO
description: Using primary and secondary texts, the course explores the evolution of postcolonialphilosopher Frantz Fanons ideas from his seminal Black Skin, White Masks (1952) and 1961The Wretched of the Earth (for which Sartre wrote the Preface) through Che GuevarasTricontinental manifesto and filmmaker Glauber Rochas positive response (written in 1967) andtheir increasing relevance to a contemporary world where racism, colonization and the necessityfor global resistance are all the more pronounced.
prerequisites_raw: UPPER-DIVISION STANDING. MAY BE REPEATED FOR CREDIT TO A MAXIMUM OF 12 UNITS

title: Cognitive Approaches to World Literature
description: Cognitive science has long recognized narrative as a basic organizing principle of our minds. Storytelling is how we make sense of the world, & the most powerful fictions of world literature are ones that give a sense of coherence. This course introduces students to key issues of world literature along with current findings on human identity in neuro-cognitive sciences. We will study significant developments in contemporary views of mind/brain, as well as read great texts of world literature through a cognitive lens. Alongside key critical & scientific articles, we will read some of the world's best stories (from 1001 Nights to Ishiguro's Never Let Me Go) as case studies for current debates in world literature & cognitive neuroscience.
prerequisites_raw: UPPER-DIVISION STANDING. MAY BE REPEATED FOR CREDIT TO A MAXIMUM OF 12 UNITS

title: Literature & Politics in China
description: Surveys politically-themed Chinese literature (in English). Studying texts from classical China, modern China, and contemporary China and Taiwan, the course encourages consideration of two questions: What makes literature on politics unique and different from, say, historical and philosophical treatises on politics? What role could literature play in politics?
prerequisites_raw: UPPER-DIVISION STANDING. MAY BE REPEATED FOR CREDIT TO A MAXIMUM OF 12 UNITS

title: Research in Translation Studies
description: Individualized instruction to complete the capstone translation project for the Minor in Translation Studies. To be completed with the faculty advisor from the language department of the student's focus.

title: Capstone Project in Childhood and Youth Studies
description: Individualized or small-group instruction to complete the capstone childhood or youth studies project for the Minor in Childhood and Youth Studies. The capstone project may be academic research, community-based work, or a creative project, with advance approval from the advisor. To be completed with a faculty advisor from a relevant department.
prerequisites_raw: Comparative Literature 128A and Comparative Literature 40 or W 40.

title: Internship
description: Under supervision of Comparative Literature faculty, Comparative Literature majors may obtain credit for work without pay in publishing, editing, journalism, or other employment related to Comparative Literature, World Literature, and/or Translation Studies. Requirements include work hours, regular meetings with professor-mentor, and a final paper presenting and analyzing the student's learning from the internship pertaining to specialization in world literary studies.
prerequisites_raw: Upper-division standing; Comparative Literature majors only; consent of department.

title: Senior Honors Independent Research
description: Student engages in research leading to a paper of considerable depth and complexity on a topic dealing with the literature of the student's focus.

title: Junior/Senior Seminar
description: Selected methodological issues in comparative literature. Topics vary with each instructor.

title: Senior Honors Seminar
description: This seminar is concurrently offered with graduate seminars. It is designed to expand research skills through an investigation of theoretical issues and readings of both literary and critical texts. It involves extensive research, sophisticated analysis, and creative reflection.

title: Independent Studies in Comparative Literature
description: Independent studies with any faculty member. To permit study of a subject desired by the student but not covered in course offerings.
prerequisites_raw: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Comparative Literature.

title: Independent Research Assistance
description: Independent research under supervision of a faculty member. May be linked to internship.
prerequisites_raw: Upper-division standing; completion of two upper-division courses in Comparative Literature; and, consent of instructor.

title: Seminar in Comparative Literature
description: Addresses issues of methodology and literary theory. Specific authors and topics vary from class to class.

title: Proseminar in Comparative Literature
description: Addresses topics relevant to comparative literary study,including scholarly approaches and practices, the discipline of comparative literature broadly conceived, and the specific resources and intellectual culture of UCSB. Course format will range from seminar style discussions, workshops, and formal presentations.

title: Critical Approaches to Comparative & World Literature
description: Explores current inquiries in literary, critical, and cognitive theories in world literatures, including the insights from transnational, intercultural, and intermedial perspectives. Topic and content will vary according to instructor.

title: Media History Theory
description: Interweaves a study of the emergence of several kinds of twentieth century media including radio, film, television, and the internet, with keytexts of media theory including Benjamin, Adorno, MdLuhan, Debord, Hall, and others.
